match.reason: No point in the bank covers the causes of workplace disputes; the closest ones, on stakeholders, the political approach and resistance to change, are related ideas rather than the same one.

draft.title: Workplace disputes
card: A workplace dispute is a disagreement between an employer and employees, or between employees and their managers. It happens when the two sides want different things or see a situation differently.
Pay is a common cause. Staff may disagree with the business over wage rates, overtime, bonuses or penalty rates.
Conditions and safety also cause disputes. Conditions include hours, rosters, breaks and leave. Safety disputes arise when staff believe a task or workplace puts them at risk of harm.
Job security and management decisions are other causes. Staff may object to redundancies, a change to casual contracts, a new roster or a restructure that they were not consulted about.
draft.remember: Disputes grow out of a clash of interests over pay, conditions, safety, job security or management decisions.

a.q: Warehouse staff at Kestrel Freight say the new loading process is unsafe, and they refuse to use it until it is changed. What is the main cause of this dispute?
a.why: The staff object because they believe the process could cause harm, which makes this a safety dispute. Pay is not the issue, because no one has raised wages or bonuses.
a.clue: What do the staff say the process might do to them?

b.q: Priya's café in Bathurst announces that three full-time baristas will be replaced by casual staff, with no change to the hourly rate. The baristas object. Which cause best describes their dispute?
b.why: The baristas fear losing their secure, ongoing positions, so the dispute is about job security. It is tempting to say pay, but the hourly rate has not changed. The management decision is the trigger, not the cause the staff are objecting to.
b.clue: The hourly rate stays the same, so what are the baristas losing?

problems.detail: The why says 'The management decision is the trigger, not the cause the staff are objecting to', but the card names management decisions as a cause of disputes and lists a change to casual contracts as an example of one. Students may be confused about whether management decisions count as a cause.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The why for (b) contradicts the card by saying a management decision is not a cause of disputes, when the card lists it as one.
